findings.headline: Growth strategy is contingent on devolution and local government reorganization, which remain uncertain external factors
findings.detail: The restructuring is explicitly designed to prepare Amphora for 'opportunities that will result for devolution and local government reorganisation'. However, the Section 151 Officer is conducting a technical review of the 5-year growth forecast to ensure it is 'sufficiently robust', suggesting scrutiny of whether growth assumptions are realistic given external dependencies.
findings.matters: The company's financial projections depend on external government decisions that may be delayed, changed, or not materialize as assumed. This creates uncertainty around whether the growth strategy will deliver planned financial performance.
findings.figures: 5-year growth forecast under technical review by Section 151 Officer
findings.quote: The proposed changes to the Amphora Group and Company structure will ensure Amphora is able to grow and realise the trading / delivery opportunities that will come through the forthcoming devolution and local government reorganisation.

findings.headline: Teckal compliance is critical infrastructure for the company's contracting model with the council
findings.detail: Teckal compliance allows the council to award work to Amphora directly without competitive procurement. The document explains that if either the control test or 80%+ activities test fails, 'the exemption fails and procurement law requires a full competitive tender', fundamentally altering the company's business model and cost-effectiveness.
findings.matters: Teckal status is essential to the company's viability as a direct service delivery vehicle. Loss of compliance could force competitive tendering, restructuring, or reversion of services to in-house council delivery.
findings.figures: 80%+ of company activities must be for the controlling authority to maintain compliance
findings.quote: If either test is not met, external trading becomes too high, or governance isn't tight enough, the exemption fails and procurement law requires a full competitive tender.

findings.headline: Implementation deadline is 31 March 2026, creating a tight 28-day window from committee approval
findings.detail: The document states changes 'will need to be implemented by 31st March 2026' (1.8). With the committee meeting on 3 March 2026, this creates intense implementation pressure across multiple moving parts: external legal advice, HMRC approval, governance document revisions, and company restructuring across three entities.
findings.matters: Tight deadlines increase execution risk. Delays or failed implementation could result in missing tax planning objectives or falling out of Teckal compliance, both with material financial consequences.
findings.figures: 31 March 2026 deadline
findings.quote: The changes will need to be implemented by 31st March 2026.

findings.headline: Council is restructuring to secure mutual trading status for tax mitigation
findings.detail: The restructuring seeks HMRC approval for mutual trading status for Amphora Services Ltd. This means surpluses from trading with the council will not be subject to Corporation Tax. Section 10.1 identifies improved tax mitigation as an immediate financial benefit of the restructuring.
findings.matters: More effective tax mitigation improves the company's financial efficiency and increases effective income available to the council from its trading operations.
findings.figures: No specific amounts stated
findings.quote: The immediate benefits of the proposed changes will be more effective tax mitigation.

findings.paper_title: Item 07(i) HRA Business Plan Update - report
findings.headline: Combined reserves came in £1.69m below forecast reducing financial cushion
findings.detail: Combined revenue and capital reserves totalled £14.28m on 1 April 2026, £1.69m less than the £15.97m estimated. This occurred because the council used Right to Buy receipt attributable debt element to finance 2025/26 rather than borrowing, a prudent choice but one that tightens available reserves.
findings.matters: Reserve levels are critical to financial resilience; lower than anticipated reserves reduce the council's ability to respond to unexpected costs or opportunities.
findings.figures: Reserves £14.28m vs £15.97m estimated; HRA debt £219.241m vs £221.000m
findings.quote: Combined revenue and capital reserves totalled £14.28m at 1 April 2026, compared to an estimated £15.97m resulting in £1.69m less opening resource overall than anticipated. This is predominantly as a result of utilising the attributable debt element of Right to Buy receipts as a financing source to reduce the need to borrow in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Item 07(i) HRA Business Plan Update - report
findings.headline: General Fund faces £1.4m temporary accommodation cost pressures forecast to continue from 2025/26 into 2026/27
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation costs in the General Fund were £1.4m in 2025/26 and would have exceeded £3.3m without containment measures. This trajectory is forecast to continue into 2026/27, placing ongoing pressure on overall council finances that could affect HRA support.
findings.matters: General Fund financial pressures can constrain councils' capacity to support HRA activities; lenders assess whole-council financial health.
findings.figures: £1.4m in 2025/26; additional £1.9m prevented through containment; £41k savings per home acquired through HRA acquisitions
findings.quote: In 2025/26 temporary accommodation cost pressures in the General Fund were £1.4m and would have been higher by £1.9m had they not been contained through Beyond the Box. This trajectory is being forecast to continue in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Item 07(i) HRA Business Plan Update - report
findings.headline: Council explicitly acknowledges current financial challenges with no investment capacity until year 8
findings.detail: The plan states there are 'current financial challenges facing the HRA' requiring careful management of forecast borrowing levels over coming years. No additional investment capacity is available until year 8, and risks are acknowledged in early years despite improved viability.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand councils' own risk assessment and the tightness of financial headroom for managing unexpected costs or opportunities.
findings.figures: No additional investment capacity until year 8
findings.quote: Given the current financial challenges facing the HRA in Colchester, with borrowing forecast to be at levels which will require careful management over the next few years, there is not currently considered to be any additional investment capacity until year 8.

findings.paper_title: Item 07(i) HRA Business Plan Update - report
findings.headline: £28.9m new Decent Homes Standard compliance costs starting 2035
findings.detail: A new regulatory standard requires substantial additional investment from 2035 onwards. The plan now incorporates these costs, with an increase of £28.9m over the 30-year plan life, though expenditure does not commence until year 11.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility of material new obligations and their long-term impact on debt sustainability and service delivery planning.
findings.figures: £28.9m increase in costs over the 30-year plan; costs incurred from year 11 onwards
findings.quote: The anticipated cost to meet the new Decent Homes Standard (DHS) from 2035 has been incorporated, with a resulting increase in cost of £28.9m over the life of the Plan, recognising that the cost will be incurred from year 11 onwards.

findings.paper_title: Item 07(i) HRA Business Plan Update - report
findings.headline: Borrowing forecast two years earlier than January 2026 plan anticipated
findings.detail: The plan shows 'prudent' borrowing against sector benchmarks will be needed after year 7, moved forward from year 9. While offset by rent convergence and lower borrowing rates, this indicates tighter financial position than previously forecast.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand councils' capital market access timing and forecast debt trajectories to assess long-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Borrowing now after year 7 vs year 9 previously
findings.quote: 'Prudent' borrowing against standard sector benchmarks now comes after year 7, compared to 9 when the baseline plan was approved in January 2026, with rent convergence and a reduction in borrowing rates more than outweighing the negative financial impact of the new DHS.

findings.paper_title: Item 08(iii) 2025-26 Year End Review of Risk Management - Report
findings.headline: Internal audit of risk management gave 'Reasonable' assurance only, with four recommendations to address gaps
findings.detail: An audit completed September 2025 rated the risk management framework as 'Reasonable' rather than a stronger assurance level. Four recommendations were issued: better definition of mitigating actions, preventing use of previously-identified risks as mitigations for other risks, improving escalation between operational and strategic registers, and developing operational risk registers further.
findings.matters: A 'Reasonable' rather than 'Strong' assurance rating indicates material gaps in the risk management framework. The specific recommendations suggest risks may lack clear definition, mitigations may be insufficiently rigorous, and escalation procedures may be weak, creating a control environment that may not catch or report emerging financial problems adequately.
findings.figures: Four recommendations
findings.quote: The Internal Audit of Risk Management was completed in September 2025 and achieved a 'Reasonable' assurance rating. Four recommendations were made relating to better definition of mitigating actions, not using a process that had been identified as a risk as a mitigating action on other risks, escalation of risks between Operational and Strategic and development of the operational risk registers.

findings.paper_title: Item 08(iii) 2025-26 Year End Review of Risk Management - Report
findings.headline: Strategic risk flagged for missing December 2026 Local Plan submission deadline
findings.detail: Risk P has been added to the strategic register identifying the risk of not submitting a Local Plan to the Planning Inspectorate by December 2026, a statutory deadline. No detail is given on the current state of the plan, likelihood of delay, or mitigation steps.
findings.matters: Missing a statutory Local Plan submission deadline can trigger government intervention or special measures, potentially affecting planning authority status and limiting the council's ability to secure development income or control strategic capital investment.
findings.figures: Submission deadline: December 2026
findings.quote: Local Plan, risk P – setting out the risks of not submitting a Local Plan to the Planning Inspectorate by December 2026

findings.paper_title: Item 08(iii) 2025-26 Year End Review of Risk Management - Report
findings.headline: Northern Gateway Leisure Park now flagged as strategic risk due to lease and funding arrangement problems
findings.detail: A new risk (risk Q) has been added to the strategic risk register specifically identifying concerns about lease and funding arrangements at Northern Gateway Leisure Park. The paper provides no further detail on what these problems are or their financial extent.
findings.matters: Leisure facilities frequently require ongoing council subsidy or capital support. Identified 'funding arrangement' risks suggest either structural insufficiency in current funding or problems requiring additional council resources or restructuring, both of which affect the authority's financial position.
findings.figures: Not provided
findings.quote: Northern Gateway Leisure Park, risk Q- setting out the risks of the lease and funding arrangements.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand significantly above target despite active interventions.
findings.detail: The temporary accommodation service experienced very high demand throughout the year, with levels remaining above the monitoring target despite interventions that prevented or relieved homelessness for 362 households. The council has formalised its approach to securing accommodation to better reflect need and case complexity, but remains focused on acquiring better low-cost temporary accommodation and identifying opportunities to mitigate future demand.
findings.matters: Sustained above-target demand for temporary accommodation indicates ongoing housing stress and could create future budgetary pressures if the underlying demand drivers persist.
findings.figures: Maintained above monitoring target; 362 households had homelessness prevented or relieved
findings.quote: The service experienced very high demand during the year, with levels remaining above the monitoring target despite proactive interventions that prevented or relieved homelessness for 362 households.

findings.headline: Business rates collection rate fell 0.59 percentage points short of target with £430k in legal write-offs from business failures.
findings.detail: The council's NNDR collection finished at 97.41% against a 98% target. The shortfall was driven by several major local businesses entering administration or ceasing trading, necessitating legal write-offs totalling over £430k. Affected businesses included River Island, Poundland, Hobbycraft, Alexander Cleghorn, and Chandlers. Similar reductions were reported by neighbouring authorities.
findings.matters: Material income shortfall combined with the failure of significant local businesses signals economic distress in the area and creates baseline uncertainty about future collection performance.
findings.figures: 0.59 percentage points below target; £430k+ in legal write-offs
findings.quote: The year end collection rate finished 0.59%pt. below the 98% target. Analysis shows this variance was primarily attributable to national economic pressures, which led to several large businesses entering administration, restructuring, or ceasing trading. As a result, legal write offs totalling over £430k were required for businesses including Alexander Cleghorn, Chandlers (Kent Blaxhill), River Island, Poundland and Hobbycraft.

findings.headline: Total external borrowing stands at £212.9m, up £22.3m in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council's debt increased from approximately £190.6m to £212.9m during the year. Of this total, £189.4m is PWLB, £13m is from other local authorities, and £10.5m from banks. The increase was planned and approved as part of the capital programme for both the general fund and HRA business plan.
findings.matters: Total debt level and composition are core metrics for assessing debt sustainability and refinancing risk.
findings.figures: £212.9m total, £189.4m PWLB, £13m inter-authority loans, £10.5m banks
findings.quote: The Council's total borrowing is £212.9m, c£189.4m was via PWLB, £13m of short-term loans from other Local Authorities and £10.5m from banks.

findings.headline: The s151 officer reports the council's treasury policy is too restrictive and lacks flexibility to respond to market shocks
findings.detail: The s151 has flagged that the current flat 30% upper limit on short-term borrowing leaves the council with very limited ability to adapt during economic stress. She notes that many other local authorities operate at 40–50% limits and has requested a review of maturity profiles to move to a more flexible laddered approach, with quarterly rather than annual monitoring.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that the council's current treasury framework may constrain its capacity to adjust borrowing strategy in response to market conditions or funding pressures.
findings.figures: Current limit 30%, peer councils use 40–50% on under-12-month debt
findings.quote: Our profile represents a very risk averse Treasury Strategy, taking a highly conservative approach to debt maturity, offering little flexibility to respond to macroeconomic market shocks.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing breached the council's 30% maturity cap at 34% in March 2026
findings.detail: External borrowing undertaken in February 2026 caused the council to exceed its self-imposed limit on short-term debt by 4%. The s151 officer reports this breach was unintentional and arose from cashflow requirements. While the indicator carries no statutory penalties, it flags that the council's debt portfolio had more exposure to interest rate fluctuations over the following 12 months than intended.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's treasury controls are working as designed and whether debt management can handle funding pressures without breaching policy.
findings.figures: 34% actual against 30% policy limit, 4% breach, £22.3m new borrowing in February
findings.quote: On 31 March 2026, there was a temporary 4% breach against the maturity limit, arising from external borrowing undertaken in February 2026. This means that our actual short-term borrowing hit 34% against a cap of 30%

findings.headline: Turnstone development was not included on strategic risk register despite significant complexity and financial exposure
findings.detail: Throughout 2024-25, despite the Turnstone leisure park showing £1.6m deficits, complex lease structures, staff turnover, and £5.2m asset-liability mismatches, no specific risk was captured on the council's strategic risk register. Internal audit was commissioned to review project governance.
findings.matters: Failure to formally identify and monitor a major financial commitment on the risk register suggests governance blind spots and prevents proper oversight by elected members and audit committee.
findings.figures: £1.6m deficit; £5.2m asset-liability mismatch; no risk register entry despite multi-year challenges
findings.quote: Throughout 2024-25, no specific risk has been included within the Council's risk register in relation to the financial and operational risks associated with the Turnstone development. Given the complexities and risks identified with this specific arrangement it is considered that the Council should be highlighting and monitoring this risk within the strategic risk register.

findings.headline: Homelessness and temporary accommodation costs continued to overspend despite mitigation efforts
findings.detail: Homelessness and temporary accommodation remains a significant budget pressure, with costs continuing to overspend in 2024-25 as part of a national trend. Council has sought out partnership arrangements with student housing providers and expanded capacity, but this represents an ongoing demand pressure.
findings.matters: A statutory obligation that is chronically overspending indicates either understated budgets or service demand that cannot be controlled, consuming reserves and reducing flexibility for other spending.
findings.figures: Homelessness/temporary accommodation identified as highest overspend area alongside corporate services
findings.quote: In line with 2023-24, homelessness/temporary accommodation costs continued to be an area of overspend within the budget. Whilst this is part of a national trend with homelessness rates increasing across the Country this remains an area of challenge for the Council.

findings.headline: Finance team heavily reliant on interim staff with forecast £1.2m overspend in 2025-26
findings.detail: Council recruited interim Section 151 Officer, Finance Director, Chief Accountant and Capital Accountant to stabilise the finance function. While this improved 2024-25 engagement, it creates risks around knowledge preservation and has created forecast overspend of £1.2m against 2025-26 budget. Previous accounts received disclaimers of opinion for 2020-21 through 2023-24.
findings.matters: Dependency on expensive interim staff for core financial roles indicates institutional weakness in financial management capability and creates sustainability concerns when interims leave.
findings.figures: £1.2m forecast 2025-26 overspend on interim staff; 4 consecutive years (2020-24) of disclaimed opinions
findings.quote: Whilst these interim roles have provided the additional capacity and experience required to stabilise the finance function within Colchester City Council, it has come with its own risks and challenges. Firstly, the reliance on interim staff has a risk in relation preservation of knowledge and skills within the team.

findings.headline: Quarterly financial reports delayed by 2–4 months, preventing timely Governance & Audit Committee decision-making
findings.detail: Governance & Audit Committee receives quarterly budget monitoring reports with at least 2 months post quarter-end delay; Q3 reporting was delayed over 4 months. Reports lack detail on cost savings progress. These delays prevent committee from making timely decisions on emerging financial issues.
findings.matters: Late financial reporting breaks the management feedback loop, preventing prompt corrective action on emerging pressures and weakening governance oversight of financial performance.
findings.figures: At least 2 months delay; Q3 report delayed 4+ months past quarter-end
findings.quote: Per review of the reporting to the Governance and Audit Committee there is at least a two month delay in the receipt of the information by the Committee. The most significant delay related to the quarter three reporting which was not received by the Committee until 5 May 2025, which was more than four months post the quarter end.

findings.headline: Council had no dedicated fraud officer or external counter fraud service during 2024-25
findings.detail: Internal audit issued an urgent recommendation that the council lacks a fraud officer or outsourced counter fraud service. Approach is reactive, relying on whistleblowing reports (only 1 received in the year). TIAA issued a limited assurance report on fraud and corruption with 1 urgent, 2 important and 1 routine recommendation in March 2025.
findings.matters: Absence of proactive fraud controls and detection capability increases risk of undetected loss or misappropriation, particularly in a council facing budget pressures.
findings.figures: 1 whistleblowing report in 2024-25; 1 urgent, 2 important recommendations from internal audit
findings.quote: KPMG note that for the 2024-25 financial year, Colchester City Council did not have an Internal Counter Fraud Officer nor did they outsource the Local Counter Fraud Service to an external provider.

findings.headline: Turnstone leisure development shows £5.2m liability excess over assets and required £4m capital subsidy from council
findings.detail: The Northern Gateway/Turnstone leisure park generated a £1.6m deficit in 2024-25. IFRS 16 valuation shows assets of £26.4m but lease liabilities of £31.6m, creating a £5.2m mismatch. The council has earmarked £4m reserves to cover lost income and separately committed an additional £4m capital contribution for cinema fit-out. Complex lease arrangements with tenants have experienced multiple changes.
findings.matters: A major capital project showing persistent losses, requiring substantial council subsidy, with unresolved lease complexity and staff turnover in project management represents a concentrated financial risk.
findings.figures: £1.6m 2024-25 deficit; assets £26.4m vs liabilities £31.6m; £4m reserves earmarked; £4m additional capital commitment
findings.quote: Within the corporate services area, there were a number of factors resulting in the overspend, most significant of which relates to a £1.6m deficit of the Northern Gateway leisure park site (Turnstone), with a specific reserve being created to cover these income shortfalls and overspends.

findings.headline: Council drew down £1.7m from reserves in 2024-25 to cover operational overspend
findings.detail: Net revenue overspend of £1.7m against budget, despite planned savings of £2.4m. Overspends of £8.6m in services were partly offset by £6.9m in corporate savings. This required a net outflow of £1.4m from usable reserves.
findings.matters: Ongoing pattern of overspending and reserve depletion reduces financial flexibility and indicates underlying structural deficit.
findings.figures: £1.7m overspend; £1.4m net outflow from usable reserves
findings.quote: Net overspend against budget for Colchester City Council 2024-25 was £1.7m. This was the result of overspends totalling £8.6m within some service lines which were offset by savings in corporate fundings and central income & expenditure (£6.9m).

findings.headline: Auditors issued a disclaimer of opinion on financial statements, unable to obtain sufficient evidence
findings.detail: KPMG could not complete necessary audit procedures across multiple areas including land and buildings valuations, investment properties (£43.2m), management override of controls, and expenditure recognition. The auditors were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence ahead of the backstop date of 27 February 2026.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion means the council's reported financial position is unvalidated. Lenders cannot verify the true financial position or judge reserve adequacy.
findings.figures: Investment properties valued at £43.2m; unable to audit multiple statement areas
findings.quote: We have issued a disclaimer of opinion on CCCs financial statements on [x] March 2026. We therefore do not express an opinion on the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Item 11(ii) - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement for 2025-26
findings.headline: Accounts historically disclaimed for years 2021-2024; progress made but auditors continue to highlight errors
findings.detail: Colchester's accounts were disclaimed for multiple years since 2021. New external auditors appointed in 2024-25 received accounts by regulatory deadline with some progress on audit matters. However, auditors continue highlighting control issues including errors in the accounts, deficient counter-fraud processes, and finance team capacity constraints.
findings.matters: A multi-year history of disclaimed accounts and ongoing accuracy issues in financial statements directly undermines credit assessment and demonstrates material accounting control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Years 2021-2024 disclaimed; ongoing errors identified in 2025-26.
findings.quote: A continuing issue in previous governance statements had been the incomplete accounts for several years since 2021, resulting in disclaimed Accounts... The auditors have however been highlighting control issues in their Value For Money assessments including: Finance team capacity... Errors in the accounts...

findings.paper_title: Item 11(ii) - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement for 2025-26
findings.headline: Northern Gateway project identified by external audit as requiring strategic risk register inclusion and ongoing risk monitoring
findings.detail: External auditors flagged Northern Gateway as a capital/major project requiring inclusion on the council's strategic risk register. The council had engaged short-term support to determine options for resolving issues with this project. An internal audit review was also carried out at the beginning of 2026-27.
findings.matters: A capital project requiring external audit flagging and remedial option review signals material delivery or financial risk that affects council balance sheet and borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: None provided in this document.
findings.quote: External Audit consider that the issues around Northern gateway should be included on the Council's strategic risk register, and this ties in with an Internal Audit review that was carried out at the beginning of 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Item 11(ii) - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement for 2025-26
findings.headline: CIPFA Financial Management Code assessment not completed due to finance team resourcing; carried forward to 2026-27
findings.detail: The council was unable to complete a full self-assessment against the CIPFA Financial Management Code in 2025-26 due to continued finance team resourcing constraints. This assessment is essential for demonstrating financial sustainability. The review will now be completed in 2026-27 after final management team appointments are made.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with the CIPFA Financial Management Code signals gaps in financial governance and sustainability planning that a lender must factor into credit decisions.
findings.figures: No figures; deferred to 2026-27.
findings.quote: Driven by various factors, chiefly limited resources in the finance team, a full assessment against the code was not possible in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Item 11(ii) - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement for 2025-26
findings.headline: Interim Chief Finance Officer in role since March 2025; permanent S151 recruitment underway
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer post is held by an Interim Chief Finance Officer appointed in March 2025, covering the entire 2025-26 financial year. Permanent recruitment is underway with an appointment expected early in 2026-27. This signals instability in the key financial leadership role.
findings.matters: The absence of a permanent chief finance officer is a governance weakness and creates risk around financial strategy continuity and stability.
findings.figures: Appointment expected early 2026-27.
findings.quote: The post of Section 151 Officer for Colchester City Council is held by the Interim Chief Finance Officer, appointed in March 2025. The permanent Chief Finance Officer (S151) recruitment is underway, with an appointment likely in early 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Item 11(ii) - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement for 2025-26
findings.headline: Fraud of £30k+ processed in 2025-26 by interim staff member due to time pressure and impersonation
findings.detail: A counterfeit invoice exceeding £30k was paid during the year after an interim member of staff with significant authority authorised it under time pressure and false Chief Executive approval. No council staff involvement was suggested. Action Fraud found insufficient evidence to pursue further. This exposed a weakness in authorisation controls and interim staffing risks.
findings.matters: A material fraud incident indicates control gaps and staffing vulnerabilities that matter directly to credit risk assessment and financial controls.
findings.quote: The Council experienced a fraud during 2025/26 when a counterfeit invoice was processed for payment. The payment was in excess of £30k. The review of the incident showed that an interim member of staff, who had significant authority, had authorised the payment.

findings.paper_title: Item 11(ii) - Appendix 1 - Draft Annual Governance Statement for 2025-26
findings.headline: Finance system at end of useful life with no upgrade path and no business ownership
findings.detail: External auditors identified an absence of business ownership for the Finance application, preventing the IT team from implementing necessary controls. The system has reached the end of its useful life with no upgrade option available. A joint options appraisal is being developed as an urgent matter with partner councils, with a recommendation expected over summer and implementation in autumn.
findings.matters: A finance system that is obsolete and lacks governance controls is a material risk to financial accuracy and timely reporting for any lender assessing borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: No figures provided; implementation timeline is summer recommendation/autumn implementation.
findings.quote: External Audit identified there is an absence of business ownership for the Finance application, resulting in the IT team unable to implement controls that necessitate business support and oversight. The system has also reached the end of its life and there is no upgrade option.

findings.paper_title: Item 7(vi) - Year End Internal Audit Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Leisure World audit shows downward trend with limited assurance and an urgent recommendation
findings.detail: Leisure World moved from a higher assurance level to limited assurance in 2025-26, with one urgent recommendation and other control issues. This represents a service deterioration within the council's audit portfolio.
findings.matters: A significant council service showing worse audit performance suggests emerging operational or financial control weaknesses that could affect service delivery or financial management.
findings.figures: Leisure World: 1 urgent recommendation, 1 important, 2 routine recommendations
findings.quote: Leisure World Limited ▼ 1 1 2 0

findings.paper_title: Item 7(vi) - Year End Internal Audit Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Limited assurance audits doubled year-on-year, with urgent recommendations tripled
findings.detail: The council received four limited assurance ratings (21% of audits) compared to two last year (9.5%), and six urgent recommendations were made compared to two last year. This represents a deterioration in audit outcomes despite an overall reasonable assurance position from the audit provider.
findings.matters: Increasing numbers of limited assurance ratings and tripled urgent recommendations suggest emerging control weaknesses that require management attention and could affect the council's operational and financial resilience.
findings.figures: Four limited assurance ratings (21%) vs two (9.5%) last year; six urgent recommendations vs two last year
findings.quote: There were four limited assurance ratings (21%), compared to two (9.5%) last year. Six urgent recommendations were made, compared to two last year.

findings.paper_title: Item 7(iii) - Treasury Management Strategy (inc. Investment Strategy) 2026-27
findings.headline: Council will borrow to fund ambitious capital programmes while facing planned dissolution
findings.detail: The council states it has ambitious capital plans in both General Fund and Housing Revenue Account programmes. It indicates borrowing will be a primary funding mechanism and that the Treasury Management Strategy sets an authorised borrowing limit. Specific project details, amounts, and timelines are not detailed in this summary.
findings.matters: Borrowing for capital immediately before the council's planned dissolution could transfer substantial inherited debt to the successor authority. Lenders need clarity on the scale of planned borrowing and how it will be managed through the structural transition.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: One of the ways to do this is by borrowing money and the Treasury management Strategy sets out how money can be borrowed, with which lenders and sets an authorised limit to borrow.

findings.paper_title: Item 7(iii) - Treasury Management Strategy (inc. Investment Strategy) 2026-27
findings.headline: Colchester will cease to exist as a separate council and merge into a larger unitary authority by 2030
findings.detail: The council acknowledges it will likely no longer be a separate sovereign entity by the end of its four-year MTFS period (31 March 2030), when Colchester becomes part of a larger unitary authority. This represents fundamental structural change occurring within the planning horizon. The council states it intends to hand over a prudent organisation without large deficits or reckless borrowing to the successor authority.
findings.matters: Organisational dissolution within the planning period is a material governance risk for lenders. It raises questions about debt assumption post-merger, financial management continuity, and whether a borrowing entity will exist for the full term of any loans extended.
findings.figures: Four-year MTFS period ending 31 March 2030
findings.quote: It is likely that the Council will no longer exist as a separate sovereign entity by the end of this MTFS period given the fact that Colchester along with other Essex authorities is likely to become part of a larger unitary authority.

findings.headline: Corporate interest underspend of c£3.6m is masking service overspend
findings.detail: The reported net surplus of c£0.2m is achieved only because a c£3.6m underspend on corporate interest and MRP payable offsets the c£3.5m service overspend. Without this interest benefit, the outturn would show a deficit covered by reserves alone.
findings.matters: Reliance on interest underspends (driven by factors outside the council's control: interest rates, actual vs. budgeted borrowing) to offset operational overspends creates financial fragility and masks underlying cost control problems.
findings.figures: Corporate Interest & MRP underspend c£3.6m; Service overspend c£3.5m
findings.quote: offset by an underspend on Corporate Income & Expenditure (Interest & MRP payable) of c£3.6m

findings.headline: Capital programme underspent by c£9.3m (33% of budget)
findings.detail: General Fund capital outturn was c£18.6m against a budget of c£28m. This £9.3m underspend is a material slippage in capital programme delivery—roughly one-third of planned capital investment did not occur.
findings.matters: Large capital underspends indicate project delays or delivery capacity constraints, which can affect the council's ability to manage infrastructure and strategic investment, and may signal cash-flow or project management issues.
findings.figures: Capital budget c£28m; outturn c£18.6m; adverse variance c£9.3m
findings.quote: The General Fund capital is an outturn of c£18.6m, an adverse position to budget of c£9.3m against a budget of c£28m.

findings.headline: Service-level overspend of c£3.5m offset by drawing c£4.3m from reserves
findings.detail: The council reports a net revenue surplus of c£0.2m, but this masks c£3.5m of service overspend. This overspend was offset by applying c£4.3m of reserves, with the remaining balance filled by corporate income underspend. This is unsustainable: reserves are being drawn down to cover day-to-day service costs rather than one-off items.
findings.matters: Recurring reliance on reserves to plug operational overspends signals that base budgets do not match service costs, reducing financial resilience and raising sustainability questions for a potential lender.
findings.figures: Service level overspend c£3.5m; Reserves applied c£4.3m; Net Surplus c£0.2m
findings.quote: At Service Level there is an overspend of c£ 3.5m (after the application of c£4.3m of Reserves)

findings.headline: General Fund capital forecast c£40.3m, adverse variance of c£0.7m against £41.0m budget
findings.detail: Capital spending is forecast at c£40.3m, which is £0.7m below the £41.0m budget. This underspend is characterised as 'adverse' which suggests capital schemes may not be progressing as planned.
findings.matters: Capital project delays or slippage can indicate programme management issues or delivery risks that affect medium-term infrastructure investment and borrowing assumptions.
findings.figures: Capital forecast c£40.3m; Budget c£41.0m; Variance c£0.7m adverse
findings.quote: The General Fund capital is forecast c.40.3m, an adverse position to budget of c£0.7m against a budget of c£41.0m.

findings.headline: Demand-led cost pressures in housing, waste, and leisure driving the deficit
findings.detail: The council specifically identifies General Fund Housing, Waste Services, and Sport & Leisure as the source of demand-led cost pressures. These are operational services that cannot easily be cut or paused.
findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends in housing and waste are structural pressures unlikely to reverse mid-year, suggesting the deficit will need active management or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: None quantified by service in this summary
findings.quote: The forecast position is driven by a number of demand -led cost pressures, particularly within General Fund Housing and operational activities such as Waste Services and Sport & Leisure.

findings.headline: General Fund revenue deficit of c£2.4m at Q1 2026-27
findings.detail: The council is reporting a net deficit of c£2.4m for the first quarter of 2026-27. Service-level overspends of c£3.8m are only partially offset by a Business Rates Pooling Benefit of c£1.4m, leaving a material deficit position.
findings.matters: A £2.4m deficit in Q1 signals either structural budget issues or uncontrolled demand pressures that lenders would want to understand and monitor through the year.
findings.figures: Net deficit c£2.4m; Service level overspend c£3.8m; Business Rates Pooling Benefit offset c£1.4m
findings.quote: At Q1 for Financial Year 2026/27, the Council is reporting a Net deficit of c£2.4m on General Fund Revenue.  At Service Level there is an overspend of c£ 3.8m, which is partially offset by a Business Rates Pooling Benefit on Corporate Income & Expenditure of (c£1.4m).

findings.paper_title: Item 7(i) - Appendix 3 - Colchester City Council ISA 260 – 2024-2025
findings.headline: CIPFA review identified lack of consistent asset governance and £14.6m of assets in wrong budgets
findings.detail: A CIPFA-commissioned review in May 2023 recommended creation of a 'corporate landlord' team to improve asset oversight. An EY report subsequently identified 475 budget lines totalling £14.6m that should be incorporated into the corporate landlord model but are currently held in service budgets. While implementation of the corporate landlord model progressed during 2024-25, auditors note the effectiveness of these changes cannot be determined until 2025-26.
findings.matters: Assets being budgeted in multiple places creates loss of visibility and inconsistent management. A £14.6m governance gap indicates the council cannot currently produce a reliable consolidated asset position, limiting confidence in asset valuations and maintenance planning.
findings.figures: £14.6m across 475 budget lines incorrectly held in service budgets
findings.quote: the report issued by EY identified 475 budget lines totalling £14.6m which should be incorporated into the corporate landlord and are currently included in service budgets

findings.paper_title: Item 7(i) - Appendix 3 - Colchester City Council ISA 260 – 2024-2025
findings.headline: Turnstone development not captured on strategic risk register throughout 2024-25 despite material transaction
findings.detail: Auditors identified through their detailed review of Turnstone arrangements that no risk was captured on the strategic risk register throughout 2024-25, and retrospective review showed it was not captured throughout the history of the transaction either. This represents a governance gap: a £26.4m+ asset revision should have been tracked as a strategic risk.
findings.matters: Risk registers exist to ensure decision-makers are aware of emerging issues. Material transactions being absent from the risk register suggests either poor governance controls or selective risk reporting, both of which undermine the council's ability to proactively manage financial exposure.
findings.figures: Turnstone transaction value £26.4m+ revision
findings.quote: As part of the detailed review of the Turnstone arrangements, it was identified that no risk was captured on the strategic risk register throughout 2024-25 and through retrospective review of risk registers has not been captured throughout the history of the transaction

findings.paper_title: Item 7(i) - Appendix 3 - Colchester City Council ISA 260 – 2024-2025
findings.headline: No dedicated fraud officer or counter-fraud service; council relies only on reactive whistle-blowing
findings.detail: The auditors found that Colchester City Council does not have a dedicated fraud officer and did not outsource local counter fraud services to an external provider during 2024-25. This was raised as an urgent recommendation by internal audit. The council's approach to fraud risk management is therefore largely reactive, relying on whistle-blowing channels rather than proactive detection or prevention.
findings.matters: Proactive fraud detection is a standard control in councils managing significant public funds and assets. Absence of this function, especially given documented staff turnover, creates heightened fraud risk. Auditors have already identified a heightened risk of management override of controls due to lack of effective fraud processes.
findings.figures: None in the paper
findings.quote: KPMG note that for the 2024/25 financial year, Colchester City Council did not have an internal fraud officer nor did the outsource the LCFS to an external provider. This was raised within the internal audit assurance review as an urgent recommendation

findings.paper_title: Item 7(i) - Appendix 3 - Colchester City Council ISA 260 – 2024-2025
findings.headline: High-risk journal entries lack documentation due to finance staff turnover and lost knowledge from ended shared service
findings.detail: Auditors identified 18 journal entries meeting high-risk criteria (impacting income recognition, cash, and expenditure). For 7 of these, insufficient documentation was retained to support the entries, attributed to high levels of staff turnover within the finance team and loss of corporate knowledge following the ending of the shared service arrangement with Epping Council. This prevents verification that entries are legitimate.
findings.matters: Inability to document and justify high-risk transactions creates exposure to fraud and error. Combined with auditors' assessment of heightened management override risk due to lack of effective fraud management processes, this represents a control environment weakness that could allow material misstatements to pass undetected.
findings.figures: 7 of 18 high-risk journals lack documentation
findings.quote: We identified 18 journal entries and other adjustments meeting our high-risk criteria – our examination identified that due to the high levels of staff turnover within the CCC finance team, insufficient documentation has been retained for 7 journals, preventing sufficient appropriate audit evidence being obtained

findings.paper_title: Item 7(i) - Appendix 3 - Colchester City Council ISA 260 – 2024-2025
findings.headline: Council has drawn down 22% of usable reserves over the last four years to balance budgets
findings.detail: The auditors noted that over the last four years the council has utilised 22% of its usable reserves to support the balanced budget. This indicates recurring deficits being masked by reserve drawdown rather than structural budget solutions. The auditors were unable to complete testing on expenditure accruals, citing concerns that the council may be understating accruals to push expenditure into future years to mitigate financial pressures.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion at this rate is unsustainable and indicates the council is living beyond its means year-on-year. If reserves continue depleting, the council will lose its only financial buffer and be forced to cut services or borrow. Lenders track reserve depletion as a leading indicator of financial distress.
findings.figures: 22% of usable reserves utilised over 4 years; Uncorrected audit misstatement £0.4m (28%) understatement of revenues deficit
findings.quote: It has been noted that over the last 4 years the Council have utilised 22% of its usable reserves to support the balanced budget

findings.paper_title: Item 7(i) - Appendix 3 - Colchester City Council ISA 260 – 2024-2025
findings.headline: Turnstone development asset revaluation of £26.4m contains material misstatements that auditors could not verify
findings.detail: The council obtained an updated valuation for Turnstone that resulted in a £26.4m revision to the asset value. Auditors identified deviations from RICS industry guidance in the valuation methodology, received poor quality evidence from management's specialist, and concluded they could not carry out sufficient testing to verify the balance. The asset was reclassified from investment property to PPE and is being disclaimed in the audit report.
findings.matters: A £26.4m asset revision indicates either prior-year mispricing or significant current-year valuation uncertainty. The auditors' inability to verify the balance, combined with deviations from industry guidance, suggests the asset may be materially misstated on either side—a critical issue for a lender assessing balance sheet quality.
findings.figures: £26.4m revision; Balance £681m for land and buildings (which includes Turnstone); £43.2m investment properties (also impacted by Turnstone reclassification)
findings.quote: Management obtained an updated valuation in respect of the Turnstone development which resulted in a £26.4m revision to the initial asset value, we consider that we have not carried out sufficient testing to conclude on these balances, and note that the balance is being disclaimed however this is indicative of material misstatements within the account balances

findings.paper_title: Item 7(i) - Appendix 3 - Colchester City Council ISA 260 – 2024-2025
findings.headline: Auditors disclaiming their opinion on the entire financial statements due to pervasive asset valuation failures
findings.detail: KPMG is issuing a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements as a whole rather than an audit opinion. The auditors were unable to complete work on land and buildings valuation (£681m), investment properties (£43.2m), management override of controls, expenditure recognition, and IFRS 16 implementation. This is one of the most serious audit outcomes possible, indicating the auditors cannot provide any assurance on the financial statements.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion means creditors, lenders, and counterparties cannot rely on the council's financial statements at all. This creates acute uncertainty about the council's true financial position and is typically followed by lender restrictions or demand for additional security.
findings.figures: Land and buildings £681m; Investment properties £43.2m; Turnstone development £26.4m revaluation
findings.quote: As a result of the pervasiveness of the above, we intend to issue a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements as a whole

findings.headline: £163m HRA borrowing concentrated in 2028–30, creating refinancing and debt sustainability risk when combined with GF borrowing
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account capital programme requires £163.1m of borrowing over 2025–31, with peak annual borrowing of £42.3m in 2028/29. Combined with GF borrowing of £53.2m over the same period, total new council debt reaches £216m+, with significant concentration in 2028–30 when MRP obligations from earlier years will also be rising.
findings.matters: The timing concentration creates refinancing risk, debt sustainability concerns, and limits future borrowing capacity; peak debt service occurs when prior MRP obligations are also growing.
findings.figures: £163.056m total HRA borrowing; £256.471m total HRA capital programme; peak annual HRA borrowing £42.258m (2028/29)

findings.headline: Holy Trinity Church project has unfunded additional spend dependent on successful external bids
findings.detail: The restoration project has confirmed spend through 2027/28, but further allocations are contingent on securing grants from National Lottery Heritage Fund and other sources. This introduces funding risk to project delivery.
findings.matters: Introduces uncertainty to capital programme delivery and suggests potential under-delivery if external funding bids are unsuccessful.
findings.figures: £2m anticipated from National Lottery Heritage Fund
findings.quote: The final spend of the project is confirmed for 2027/28, with additional allocations contingent on successful external bids.

findings.headline: Northern Gateway Leisure Park requires £6.5m additional investment beyond base programme, described as critical to project success
findings.detail: Beyond the capital programme, £6.5m is required to enable the anchor tenant to sign a long lease. The strategy describes this as necessary to provide 'confidence to existing and future tenants' and states it is 'critical to the success of the wider development', suggesting project viability depends on securing this additional investment.
findings.matters: This indicates scope change and additional borrowing need that may not have been fully factored into baseline forecasts, and uses language suggesting the scheme cannot proceed without it.
findings.figures: £6.5m additional investment (£0.5m for other units)
findings.quote: An additional £6.5m investment is included to enable the anchor tenant to sign a long lease (of which £0.5m is for other units), supporting the sustainability of the site. This investment will provide confidence to existing and future tenants and is critical to the success of the wider development.

findings.headline: £53.2m GF borrowing requirement over MTFF with uncertain revenue impact from MRP fluctuation
findings.detail: The council will borrow £10.8m in 2025/26, £16.4m in 2026/27, and £53.2m over the full medium-term financial forecast to fund capital projects. The strategy explicitly warns that Minimum Revenue Provision costs 'will fluctuate throughout the life of the capital programme, depending on changes in expenditure and funding' and 'directly impacts the Council's bottom line'.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility of how fluctuating MRP obligations will constrain future revenue budgets and affect sustainability of the borrowing programme.
findings.quote: MRP is included within the annual capital financing budget and replaces other accounting charges, such as depreciation, in the Council's Statement of Accounts. It directly impacts the Council's bottom line and will fluctuate throughout the life of the capital programme, depending on changes in expenditure and funding.

findings.headline: Colchester appoints permanent Section 151 Officer after interim stabilisation period
findings.detail: Tina French is appointed as Section 151 Officer effective 21 September 2026. The previous interim S151 Officer, Anna D'Alessandro, was appointed to stabilise the finance function. The council states this stabilisation has now been completed. Tina is described as an experienced finance director with extensive District and County Council experience.
findings.matters: Changes in Chief Finance Officer are material to lenders assessing governance and financial management. The explicit reference to the finance function requiring prior stabilisation indicates the council previously had financial administration issues.
findings.figures: Effective from 21 September 2026
findings.quote: Anna was appointed as interim S151 officer to allow a period of stabilisation of the finance function. This has now happened and we now have clarity about our future configuration for local government reorganisation.

findings.paper_title: Item 08(i) Budget 2026-27 and Medium-Term Financial Forecast report
findings.headline: Minimum General Fund contingency balance set at £3.5 million
findings.detail: The S151 Officer has recommended and Cabinet is asked to approve maintaining a minimum contingency balance of £3.5 million in the General Fund Reserve. This is the floor for financial resilience against unforeseen pressures.
findings.matters: The adequacy of reserves is a direct indicator of financial resilience. A lender will want to know whether this minimum is being maintained, depleted, or whether pressures are pushing the council below it.
findings.figures: £3.5 million minimum contingency balance
findings.quote: the Section 151 Officer's recommendation to maintain a minimum £3.5 million contingency balance in the Council's General Fund Reserve be approved

findings.paper_title: Item 08(i) Budget 2026-27 and Medium-Term Financial Forecast report
findings.headline: Chief Finance Officer position is held on interim basis
findings.detail: The S151 Officer role is titled 'Interim Chief Finance Officer'. This suggests a staffing transition or vacancy in the permanent position. Given the complexity of the planned reorganisation and the need for robust financial stewardship during budget pressures, interim leadership of the finance function is a governance concern.
findings.matters: Stability in senior finance leadership is material to lenders assessing financial governance and decision-making quality, particularly during significant structural change.
findings.figures: Interim Chief Finance Officer (S151) Wayne Layton
findings.quote: Interim Chief Finance Officer (S151) Wayne Layton

news_drafts.headline: Growth strategy is contingent on devolution and local government reorganization, which remain uncertain external factors
news_drafts.lead: The company's financial projections depend on external government decisions that may be delayed, changed, or not materialize as assumed. This creates uncertainty around whether the growth strategy will deliver planned financial performance.

news_drafts.headline: Teckal compliance is critical infrastructure for the company's contracting model with the council
news_drafts.lead: Teckal status is essential to the company's viability as a direct service delivery vehicle. Loss of compliance could force competitive tendering, restructuring, or reversion of services to in-house council delivery.

news_drafts.headline: Implementation deadline is 31 March 2026, creating a tight 28-day window from committee approval
news_drafts.lead: Tight deadlines increase execution risk. Delays or failed implementation could result in missing tax planning objectives or falling out of Teckal compliance, both with material financial consequences.
